title: David Cronenberg
subtitle: the directed features, in release order
blurb: Every feature he directed, Stereo to The Shrouds — 55 years of flesh, machines and Canadian film money, about 38 hours.
notes: The filmography, not a body-horror canon.

This list was proposed two ways: his films, or a canon of the genre he is credited with originating. It is his films, because a body-horror canon would be mostly him anyway — better to have the filmography first and let the canon spend its rows on everyone else, with this page carrying the spine.
Features only. The television is not here.

He directed for television and none of it is on this list. What that leaves out is nine documentary shorts he made for the CBC in 1971 and 1972, and single episodes or pairs of episodes of five series that belong to other people — Program X, Peep Show, Teleplay, Friday the 13th: The Series and Scales of Justice. An episode of somebody else's anthology is not a film of his. The seven short films are out on the same grounds, as are the commercials, and so is his long second career acting in other directors' pictures.
The four sections are Wikipedia's, not ours.

His biography splits its Career section four ways — film debut and early work, breakthrough and acclaim, career fluctuations, resurgence — and this list takes those year ranges as its era boundaries rather than inventing its own. The generator reads the headings and fails if they change, so the divisions on this page cannot quietly stop matching the article they came from.

Every row is weighted, in hours, from the runtime published in that film's own Wikipedia infobox — never from an average and never estimated. The shortest is Crimes of the Future (1970) at 63 minutes and the longest The Shrouds (2024) at 120.

Roster from Wikipedia's David Cronenberg filmography, read from the Film table itself; era boundaries from the career headings on the David Cronenberg article; runtimes and release dates from each film's own article.

sections.title: The early Canadian films
sections.intro: Two art-house features shot around Toronto without synchronised sound, then a partnership with Ivan Reitman and a decade of Canadian government financing. The body-horror pictures that made his name are here, and so is the drag-racing film he made in the middle of them because he liked cars.

items.note: Shot in black and white without synchronised sound, on the University of Toronto's Scarborough campus — he directed, wrote, shot, cut and produced it
The second art-house feature, in colour and again a one-man crew; it shares a title with the 2022 film and nothing else
His first commercial feature, part-financed by the taxpayer-funded CFDC — which is how it ended up debated in Parliament
Marilyn Chambers took the lead after Sissy Spacek, his first choice, did not; the film that won him international distributors
A drag-racing picture made between Rabid and The Brood, out of his own interest in cars and bike gangs
The first of his films scored by Howard Shore, who has scored every one since bar The Dead Zone

sections.title: Breakthrough and acclaim
sections.intro: Five films in eight years, the run that took him from cult director to one studios would hand a remake to. Howard Shore scored all but one of them, and from the last of them on, Peter Suschitzky has shot every film he has made.

items.note: He started shooting without a finished script, writing that day's scenes in the mornings; he calls it his hardest film to make
Universal put up half the budget and distributed it, on the strength of a one-page description
From Stephen King's 1979 novel, and the one film since 1979 Howard Shore did not score — Michael Kamen did
A remake of Kurt Neumann's 1958 film and his biggest hit at $60 million; he directed Shore's opera of it in 2008
The start of the run with cinematographer Peter Suschitzky, who has shot every film he has made since

sections.title: Naked Lunch to Spider
sections.intro: The stretch of adaptations nobody thought could be adapted — Burroughs, Hwang's play, Ballard — with an original of his own in the middle of it. Two of the five were shot outside Ontario, which for him is unusual.

items.note: Partly from William S. Burroughs' 1959 novel, long called unfilmable, and partly from Burroughs' own life
David Henry Hwang adapted his own 1988 play, and most of it was shot in China — for Cronenberg, unusually far from Ontario
From J. G. Ballard's 1973 novel; the Cannes jury made a Special Jury Prize for it, for originality and daring
The one original screenplay in this stretch — the four films around it are all adaptations
From Patrick McGrath's novel, shot in England on a small budget with part of his own fee deferred

sections.title: The resurgence
sections.intro: Bigger budgets, mostly other people's scripts, and four films with Viggo Mortensen. Twenty years wide, with an eight-year gap in the middle of it during which he published a novel and was reported to be considering retirement, and two late films back in Cannes competition.

items.note: One of his largest budgets, and the first of four films with Viggo Mortensen
Filmed mostly in England, and his second with Mortensen
From Christopher Hampton's play The Talking Cure, shot in Germany and Austria
From Don DeLillo's 2003 novel, and in competition at Cannes
The first film he shot in the United States, after four decades of working at home
Shot in Greece after an eight-year gap, and unrelated to the 1970 film of the same name
Premiered in Cannes competition and reached cinemas that September
